Yes—under those conditions, you would very likely be able to spot the Moon.

- It is **6.78° above the eastern-southeastern horizon** (azimuth ~104°), so it is physically above the horizon.
- At **96.97% illumination** and **159.91° from the Sun**, it is essentially a bright, nearly full Moon. Its brightness is roughly comparable to a full Moon, though slightly less.
- The Sun is only **3° above the western horizon**, so the sky is still bright, which reduces contrast. But a nearly full Moon is bright enough to remain visible in daylight, especially with clear skies.
- At an altitude of nearly 7°, local obstructions—trees, buildings, hills, haze near the horizon—could easily hide it. If your view toward azimuth 104° is unobstructed, though, an ordinary observer who knows where to look would probably find it.

So: **not guaranteed from every location because it is low and the sky is bright, but very likely visible with a clear, unobstructed view.** Look about 7° above the horizon toward the east-southeast—roughly the width of a closed fist held at arm’s length above the horizon.
